content.intro: This lesson focuses on building a self-hosted runner environment. A self-hosted runner fleet needs controlled registration, an up-to-date machine image, required tooling, restricted network access, and health monitoring. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Building a Self-Hosted Runner Environment matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. A self-hosted runner fleet needs controlled registration, an up-to-date machine image, required tooling, restricted network access, and health monitoring. Self-hosted runners provide control but widen the operational responsibility. Restrict access, isolate trust levels, patch images, remove residual state, and monitor fleet health.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain building a self-hosted runner environment, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Treat self-hosted runner machines as privileged infrastructure with lifecycle, network, and isolation needs.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: A self-hosted runner fleet needs controlled registration, an up-to-date machine image, required tooling, restricted network access, and health monitoring. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
